analysis.one_liner: Lets people erase their personal data from every data broker with one free government-run request.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the Senate Commerce Committee without ever getting a vote, leaving data brokers free to sell personal information with no centralized way to opt out.
analysis.plain_summary: The DELETE Act would have required data brokers — companies that buy and sell people's personal information without a direct relationship with them — to register with the Federal Trade Commission and disclose what data they collect. It would have created a free website where a person could submit one request, through secured hashed lists, to have every registered data broker delete their information and stop collecting it. Companies would have had about a month to comply after each match, with independent audits and FTC enforcement.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people whose personal data — names, addresses, browsing histories, locations, inferences about their habits and finances — is bought and sold by data brokers they have never dealt with. Instead of hunting down dozens of companies one by one, they could submit one free request to the FTC and every registered broker holding their identifiers would have to delete the data and stop collecting it. People whose leaked or scraped information fuels identity theft, stalking, and targeted scams would benefit most.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Everyone whose data is sold online

how_it_helps.text: The bill would create a free, single online request through the FTC that reaches every registered data broker holding the person's identifiers, rather than forcing people to find and contact dozens of companies separately.

Data brokers would have to check hashed registries every 31 days and delete matching records within 31 days, including stopping all future collection — so one request covers brokers the person has never heard of and brokers that start operating later.

The bill requires data brokers to register annually with the FTC, disclose what data they collect and where it comes from, submit to independent third-party audits every three years, and report completion rates — the first time the largely hidden broker industry would be inventoried publicly.

The system uses salted, hashed registries so individuals' actual identifiers are not stored in readable form, and data brokers pay the operating cost through capped annual fees, so no public money is required.

analysis.who_pays: Data brokers — companies that profit from selling information about people with whom they have no relationship. They would bear registration, reporting, audit, and fee costs, and would lose revenue when deletion requests wipe their records of individuals who opt out. Marketers and advertisers that buy broker data would also lose a supply of targets.
analysis.who_pays_short: Data brokers and marketers who buy their data

drawbacks.text: The centralized system requires people to submit their email, phone number, and address to a government-run registry, which — even though the bill requires the data to be salted and hashed — creates a sensitive federal database that could itself become a target for misuse or breach.

The bill only covers data brokers trading in other people's data; companies that collect and monetize data from their own customers are not covered, and the fraud-prevention and news exemptions mean much profiling activity continues regardless of any deletion request.
The preemption clause preserves stronger state laws, but a federal system could still complicate the patchwork of state privacy rights that some states have built.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits to individuals are real: a one-stop deletion request replaces an exhausting chase across dozens of brokers, and the hashed registries keep the government from holding a list of everyone who opted out. The main drawbacks are the federal system itself, which becomes a honeypot of contact details worth attacking, and the possibility that a single deletion standard becomes a ceiling for federal regulation. The bill does not cover companies that trade in data collected from their own customers, so a large share of profiling would continue untouched. On balance it would be a meaningful privacy win for consumers at a modest cost to the data broker industry.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Commerce Committee, which never acted on it, so it expired without a vote when that Congress ended.

narrative.text: The bill's only action after introduction was being read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on June 22, 2023.
The bill never received a hearing, a committee vote, or a floor vote in the 118th Congress, which ended January 3, 2025.
The bill had two Democratic cosponsors plus its Republican sponsor, giving it support from both parties.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Data brokers, who keep selling personal information without any centralized opt-out.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Data brokers keep selling personal data

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan in sponsorship — a Republican sponsor and Democratic cosponsors — but it never advanced far enough for a vote that would show the chamber's actual split.

industries.note: The bill forces brokers to register with the FTC, disclose their data practices, honor a single centralized deletion request for everyone on the hashed registries, pay system operating fees, and submit to audits. Their core business — selling profiles of people who never signed up — would shrink sharply.
Advertisers that buy broker lists for targeted marketing would lose a key data source, raising their costs. The bill exempts firms that verify identity or prevent fraud, so some data flows continue.

industries.industry: Credit reporting agencies and fraud-prevention firms
industries.note: Consumer reporting agencies and fraud-verification services are explicitly exempt from the definition of data broker, keeping their existing role in the credit and identity-verification system intact.
